passage: You asked for a time someone said sorry properly? Okay. My mum, Farida. Before my board exams she screamed at me in front of my cousins about my mock marks, said I'd never amount to anything. I stayed at a friend's place that night. The next evening she came to pick me up. In the car she didn't even turn the radio on. She just said, "Omkar, what I said yesterday was cruel and untrue. I was scared about your exams, but that's mine to handle, not an excuse. I'm sorry." No "but you also". Nothing. I didn't know what to say, so I said "okay". We got pani puri on the way home. Weird thing is, I trust her more now than before the fight.

qa.q: Where did Omkar stay the night of the fight?
qa.a: Omkar stayed at a friend's place that night.

qa.q: How did Omkar feel when Farida apologised in the car, and what shows it?
qa.a: Omkar was surprised and unsure, not knowing what to say and managing only "okay".

qa.q: What made Farida's apology work?
qa.a: She named exactly what she had said, called it cruel and untrue, and said sorry without blaming Omkar, so it was a real repair.

qa.q: What might it have cost Farida to say sorry without excuses?
qa.a: She had to admit her own fear and set aside her pride, which is probably hard for a parent.

grounding: A teenager describes a mother who shouted cruelly, then came back, named it and apologised without excuses, which deepened trust.

passage: I'm Dolma, from the flat below. In the spring Farhan's father went away for work for three months and barely called. Farhan, fifteen, stopped coming to our evening football. When his father came back, I heard shouting at first, Farhan yelling, "You didn't even ring on my birthday!" Then the next evening I saw them on the stairs. His father was sitting two steps below him, saying, "You're right. I wasn't there, and I didn't call. That's on me, not the job. I'm sorry." Farhan didn't say anything. But on Sunday he was back at football, and his father stood at the edge of the field, watching the whole match.

qa.q: What did Farhan shout at his father?
qa.a: He yelled, "You didn't even ring on my birthday!"

qa.q: What might Farhan have been feeling when he stopped coming to football?
qa.a: He may have felt hurt and let down by his father's absence, and pulled away from things.

qa.q: What did the father's apology include that made it a real repair?
qa.a: He named what had happened, took the blame himself rather than blaming the job, and said sorry.

qa.q: How might Farhan's father feel watching the whole match on Sunday?
qa.a: He may feel relieved and grateful that Farhan is back, and keen to show he is present now.

grounding: A neighbour sees an absent father return, name his failure and apologise without excuses, and his teenage son slowly re-engage.

passage:
9 November.
Mohit was late today. Twenty minutes. Old me would have spiralled: he's bored of me, he's found someone better, typical. I felt it start, that cold drop. Then I remembered the last eight months. Every Sunday he has turned up. When he can't, he texts. Once he rode across Pune in the rain because I panicked about my scholarship. So I wrote on my hand: "Evidence says traffic." And it was traffic. He came in grumbling about a lorry. Dr Kulkarni says I'm rewriting the rulebook my childhood gave me, where promises broke all the time. It's slow. But tonight I just said "Chai?" instead of crying.
Aadhya

qa.q: How late was Mohit?
qa.a: He was twenty minutes late.

qa.q: What did Aadhya feel when Mohit was late, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Aadhya felt a cold drop of fear and began thinking Mohit was bored or had found someone better.

qa.q: What turning point helped Aadhya stay calm?
qa.a: Aadhya remembered eight months of Mohit turning up and wrote "Evidence says traffic", using his past reliability to check the old fear.

qa.q: How might Mohit experience Aadhya's simple "Chai?" compared with the old spiral?
qa.a: He probably feels relaxed and trusted rather than accused, which makes being late less stressful for him.

grounding: A young adult with an unreliable childhood uses a partner's steady track record and therapy to calm an old fear of abandonment.

passage:
In the college library's group-study room, Ishita dropped her bag on the table. "Pranav, you vanished for four days. The presentation is tomorrow."
Pranav winced. In psych elective they had just done attachment styles, and a classmate had joked, "Avoidant, so not my fault!" It would be easy to say that now.
"I know. When our group chat got tense, I did my usual thing and went quiet. With my cousins I don't, but under pressure I do. That explains it. It doesn't excuse it." He opened his laptop. "My four slides are done, and I'll do the conclusion too. Next time I'll say I need an hour instead of disappearing."
Ishita sat down. "Okay. Show me the slides."

qa.q: How long had Pranav been missing from the group?
qa.a: He vanished for four days.

qa.q: Why did Pranav wince when Ishita spoke?
qa.a: He felt guilty, knowing he had let the group down right before the presentation.

qa.q: What choice did Pranav make instead of hiding behind a label?
qa.a: He explained his tendency to go quiet under pressure but said it was no excuse, finished his slides, took on the conclusion and promised to ask for an hour next time.

qa.q: How might Ishita have reacted if Pranav had said "Avoidant, not my fault"?
qa.a: She would probably have been more frustrated, since the label would dodge responsibility for the missing work.

grounding: A student uses the idea of attachment style to understand his withdrawal, notes it varies by setting, and still takes responsibility.

passage:
Dear Harsha,
After our fight on Saturday you said, "That's just my anxious attachment, you knew that when we started." I've been thinking about it all week.
I read the same book you did, and I think it's useful. It helps me see why a late reply hits you so hard, and why I go stiff when you get upset. But I don't think either of us is only a type. You're calm as anything with your students at the tuition centre. I'm not distant with my sister.
So can we use it as a map, not a verdict? I'll own that I went quiet for a whole day. Can you own the twelve messages?
I want to keep going. Just with both of us taking our share.
Tejas

qa.q: Where is Harsha calm with students?
qa.a: At the tuition centre.

qa.q: What was Tejas worried about after Harsha pointed to attachment style?
qa.a: Tejas worried the label was being used as a verdict and an excuse, so neither of them would take responsibility.

qa.q: What turning point does Tejas propose in the letter?
qa.a: Tejas suggests treating attachment styles as a map rather than a verdict, owning a day of silence and asking Harsha to own the twelve messages.

qa.q: How might Harsha feel reading "Can you own the twelve messages?"
qa.a: Harsha may feel stung at first but also respected, since Tejas owns a share first and says the relationship is worth continuing.

grounding: A young adult writes that attachment styles vary with context and help explain reactions but do not excuse behaviour on either side.

passage: I'm Madhuri's younger brother, and I've shared a flat with her and Jeevan since June. I've watched the same loop maybe ten times. Something small goes wrong, like Jeevan forgetting to call from a work trip. Madhuri asks what's wrong, then asks again, louder. Jeevan says "Nothing," and goes to the balcony. She follows. He puts his earphones in. She cries; he goes for a drive. Last Sunday something changed. Madhuri drew two arrows on the fridge whiteboard, one chasing, one running, making a circle. "This is us," she said. "Not you, not me. Us." Jeevan actually laughed. Then he stayed at the table. I don't know what they were feeling inside, but they talked for an hour.

qa.q: What did Madhuri draw on the fridge whiteboard?
qa.a: She drew two arrows, one chasing and one running, making a circle.

qa.q: What might Madhuri be feeling when she asks again, louder?
qa.a: She may feel anxious and shut out, needing reassurance that nothing is wrong between them.

qa.q: What was the turning point on Sunday, and why did it help?
qa.a: Madhuri showed the loop as "us", not one person's fault, which let Jeevan relax and stay to talk.

qa.q: How might Jeevan see the whiteboard drawing?
qa.a: He may feel relieved not to be blamed, which is why he laughs and stays at the table.

grounding: A brother watches a couple's pursue-and-withdraw loop and sees it ease once they treat it as a shared pattern rather than one person's fault.

passage:
Diwali weekend: At the family lunch, Chetan watched his cousin Irawati and her husband Deven. Irawati kept asking why Deven was so quiet; the more she asked, the further he retreated, until he was on the terrace with the kids.
Two weeks later: Chetan had them over for dinner and saw it again, only faster. Afterwards Irawati cried in his kitchen. "Why does he always run?" Chetan said carefully, "Maybe you both have a part. You chase when he goes quiet, he goes quiet when you chase. Like a see-saw."
New Year's Eve: At the party, when Deven went quiet, Irawati said lightly, "See-saw moment?" Deven smiled. "Yes. Give me ten minutes, then I'm back." He came back in ten.

qa.q: Where did Deven retreat to at the Diwali lunch?
qa.a: He retreated to the terrace with the kids.

qa.q: What was Irawati feeling when she cried in Chetan's kitchen?
qa.a: She felt hurt and frustrated, believing Deven always runs from her.

qa.q: What turning point did Chetan offer, and why did it help?
qa.a: He described the pattern as a see-saw they both take part in, which let them spot it together instead of blaming one person.

qa.q: How might Deven feel when Irawati says "See-saw moment?" lightly?
qa.a: He probably feels understood rather than chased, so he can say what he needs and come back.

grounding: Over several weeks, a cousin watches a pursue-and-withdraw loop and helps the couple see it as a shared pattern, which opens a way out.

passage: In Seville, ten-year-old Mateo ran home waving his maths test. "A ten! Hana, look!" His big sister clapped, and he glowed all evening. On Thursday the spelling test came back with a six. Mateo stuffed it in his bag and wouldn't come to dinner. "I'm just stupid," he said into his pillow. "I'm not good at anything." Hana sat on the edge of his bed. "On Monday you were a genius and today you're stupid? You're the same Mateo." He didn't look up. "It doesn't feel like that."

qa.q: What mark did Mateo get on the spelling test?
qa.a: He got a six.

qa.q: Why does Mateo feel "stupid" after one spelling test?
qa.a: He seems to feel worthwhile only when he scores high, so one poor mark feels like proof he isn't good enough.

qa.q: What could Hana or his parents try in the weeks ahead?
qa.a: They could notice his effort and kindness, not just his marks, so his sense of worth stops rising and falling with each test.

qa.q: What is it like for Hana to see Mateo glow on Monday and crumble on Thursday?
qa.a: It is probably confusing and sad for her, because she sees him as the same brother either way.

grounding: A ten-year-old feels valuable after a high mark and crumbles after a low one, treating an ordinary setback as proof he is not enough.

passage: At the Jaipur school's quiz finals, Yogesh, eleven, stood frozen on the stage when the host announced that his team had come second. Everyone clapped. Yogesh didn't. Backstage he kicked a chair and hissed, "Second is losing. Papa only puts first prizes on the fridge." Urmila ma'am, the quiz coach, found him behind the curtain, cheeks wet. "You answered the hardest question of the day," she said. "I watched you work it out." He shook his head. "Doesn't count. We didn't win." Urmila ma'am sat on the step beside him and said nothing more for a while.

qa.q: Which place did Yogesh's team get?
qa.a: They came second.

qa.q: What does Yogesh's "Second is losing" suggest about how he sees himself?
qa.a: It suggests he feels worthwhile only when he wins, so even a good result feels like failure.

qa.q: What might help Yogesh after a day like this?
qa.a: Adults could keep pointing out his effort and thinking, as Urmila ma'am did, and his family could celebrate more than first prizes.

qa.q: How might Yogesh's teammates feel if he calls second place losing?
qa.a: They might feel their good result is being dismissed, and some may feel less proud.

grounding: An eleven-year-old whose worth depends on winning treats second place as failure, even when a coach praises his thinking.

passage:
Sunday: Dhruv, nine, refused to open the new chess puzzle book. "I'll just get them wrong." His father, Yash, said, "You found a clever trap in yesterday's game. Want to try one puzzle, just to see?"
Wednesday: Dhruv lost three games in a row to his cousin. Yash didn't mention the losses. "I saw you slow down and check each move before touching the piece. That's a strategy." Dhruv shrugged, but he set the board up again.
The next Saturday: At the colony chess club, Dhruv picked the hardest puzzle on the board. He got it wrong twice. "Third try," he muttered, grinning. When a younger boy cried after losing, Dhruv gave him half his biscuit. Yash noticed that too. "That was kind."

qa.q: What did Dhruv give the younger boy?
qa.a: He gave him half his biscuit.

qa.q: What was Dhruv afraid of on Sunday?
qa.a: He was afraid of getting the puzzles wrong, so he didn't want to try.

qa.q: Which kind of praise did Yash choose, and why did it help?
qa.a: He praised Dhruv's strategy of checking moves and later his kindness, not wins, so Dhruv felt safe to try hard puzzles.

qa.q: How might the younger boy at the chess club see Dhruv?
qa.a: He may see Dhruv as kind and friendly, someone who makes losing feel less lonely.

grounding: Over a week, a father praises his son's strategy and kindness rather than results, and the boy starts risking hard puzzles.

passage: Listen, beta. When I, Amandeep, was headmistress at the Ludhiana school, we had a boy called Siddharth, ten, who hid his drawings because his first one had been laughed at. His class teacher, Mrs Bajwa, never said "beautiful" or "talented". She would say, "You tried three shades of green for that tree. Why?" Or, "You helped Rinku with his colours. That was generous." Slowly he stopped hiding his sheets. The next year he entered the district painting contest. He didn't win anything. He came to my office anyway, beaming, and said, "Ma'am, I tried water colours for the first time!" That boy teaches art now, in Amritsar.

qa.q: What did Siddharth try for the first time at the district contest?
qa.a: He tried water colours for the first time.

qa.q: How did Siddharth feel after the contest, even without a prize, and what shows it?
qa.a: He felt proud and happy; he came to the office beaming to share what he had tried.

qa.q: What choice did Mrs Bajwa make in her praise, and why did it work?
qa.a: She asked about his colour choices and praised his generosity instead of calling him talented, so he learned that trying mattered more than results.

qa.q: How might Rinku have felt when Siddharth helped with his colours?
qa.a: He probably felt supported and grateful, and less alone in class.

grounding: A retired headmistress recalls a teacher praising a boy's effort, choices and kindness, which let him risk trying and enjoy it without winning.

passage:
Coach's note, Divyansh, Under-16 swimming squad.
Pranav talked big again today. "Butterfly's for show-offs. I could do it easy, I just don't want to." He mocked Ronit's slow turns so loudly the whole lane heard. But when I asked him to try one length of butterfly, he found three reasons to go to the washroom.
I don't think this is arrogance. I think he's scared of looking bad in front of everyone. So after practice, with the pool empty, I asked if he'd try butterfly with just me: no timing, no audience. He nearly laughed it off, then nodded. He swallowed a lot of water. He came back for a second length anyway.
Plan: two quiet sessions a week. No lectures.

qa.q: How many reasons did Pranav find to go to the washroom?
qa.a: He found three reasons to go to the washroom.

qa.q: What might Pranav be afraid of underneath the loud talk?
qa.a: He may be scared of looking bad in front of everyone if he tries and fails.

qa.q: What choice did Divyansh make instead of a lecture, and why did it work?
qa.a: Divyansh offered Pranav a private try with no timing or audience, a safe chance to fail, so Pranav tried and even came back for more.

qa.q: How might Ronit feel when Pranav mocks his slow turns?
qa.a: Ronit may feel embarrassed and small in front of the whole lane.

grounding: A coach sees a teenager's boasting and mockery as cover for fear of failing in public and offers a safe, private chance to try.

passage:
Tuesday.
In drama today I told everyone the audition piece was childish and I wasn't going to waste my time on it. Sunaina laughed at my joke, her hand over her mouth, and I felt great for about five seconds. Then Ms Almeida said, "Fine, you can prompt from the wings." So I sat there watching Sunaina and the others be awful and brilliant, and I wanted to be up there so badly my stomach hurt. Truth is, if I try and I'm bad, everyone will know I'm not as good as I act. Sunaina texted after: "You'd be good. Do the reading on Friday with me? Just us two first." Just us two first. Maybe.
Dhruv

qa.q: What did Ms Almeida tell Dhruv to do?
qa.a: She told Dhruv to prompt from the wings.

qa.q: What was Dhruv afraid of beneath calling the audition childish?
qa.a: Dhruv was afraid that trying and being bad would show everyone Dhruv is not as good as the act suggests.

qa.q: What does Sunaina's offer give Dhruv, and why might it work?
qa.a: She offers a practice reading with just the two of them first, a safe chance to try without an audience.

qa.q: How might Sunaina see Dhruv's big talk in class?
qa.a: She laughed at the joke, but her text suggests she sees that Dhruv wants to take part and believes Dhruv would be good.

grounding: A teenager mocks an audition to avoid being seen failing, admits the fear in a diary and is offered a safe first try.

passage: Your chechi Binita was fifteen when she got that photo app, mone. Your grandpa Jomon watched it all. Every night she would lie on the sofa scrolling other girls' holidays and perfect skin, and her face would go flat. If a photo got fewer hearts than her friend's, she deleted it. One evening she said, "Appachan, everyone's life is better than mine." I didn't lecture her. I just asked her to help with the church choir's Christmas concert, since she sings well. She came to practice every week. On the night she sang the solo, and her school friends came and shouted her name. After that I noticed she scrolled less. She'd say, "Can't, practice."

qa.q: What would Binita do if a photo got fewer hearts than her friend's?
qa.a: She deleted it.

qa.q: What does Binita's flat face while scrolling suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt low and behind, comparing herself with other girls' holidays and perfect skin.

qa.q: What turning point did the choir concert bring?
qa.a: Singing the solo with her real friends cheering gave her worth she could feel offline, and after that she scrolled less.

qa.q: How might Jomon have felt when Binita said everyone's life was better than hers?
qa.a: He was probably worried and sad, which is why he looked for something real she could shine at instead of lecturing.

grounding: A grandfather recalls a fifteen-year-old whose mood rose and fell with likes, and how singing with friends gave her firmer ground.

passage: The school trek to Kalsubai had one bar of signal, Omkar's battery was at nine percent, and he was panicking. He'd posted a gym photo that morning and it had only fourteen likes. Aparna's post had two hundred. "Everyone thinks I'm a joke," he muttered, holding the phone up to the grey sky. "Your phone's going to die anyway," Aparna said, pulling up her hood. "Help me with the tent?" The phone died at the second pole. They got the tent up in the drizzle, badly, then properly, laughing when it collapsed on Aparna. That night by the lantern, their teacher said theirs was the best-pitched tent in the group. Omkar realised he hadn't thought about the likes in hours.

qa.q: How many likes did Omkar's gym photo get?
qa.a: It got fourteen likes.

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling when he held the phone up to the sky, and why?
qa.a: He felt anxious and embarrassed, thinking everyone saw him as a joke because his post had fewer likes than Aparna's.

qa.q: What turning point came once the phone died?
qa.a: He joined Aparna in pitching the tent, and the shared effort and the teacher's praise gave him firmer ground than likes.

qa.q: How might Aparna have seen Omkar's worry about likes?
qa.a: She seemed to see it as less important than what was in front of them, and gently pulled him into doing something together.

grounding: On a trek with a dying phone, a teenager who measures himself by likes finds firmer ground in a shared task and a friend.

passage:
Class teacher's note, 9C, by Mrs D'Souza.
For weeks Shalini has been saying "I'm so dumb" after every answer, and today she refused to try out for the science quiz team. I watched her friend Alka handle it. Alka didn't say "Don't be silly." She said, "You explained the magnet question to me yesterday better than the textbook did." She kept sitting beside Shalini at lunch.

qa.a: She had explained the magnet question.

qa.q: What might Shalini be feeling when she keeps saying "I'm so dumb"?

qa.q: What choices did Alka make as a friend, and why were they wise?
qa.a: She gave honest, specific praise, stayed beside Shalini, and brought her to a trusted adult when the low mood lasted.

qa.q: How might Shalini feel when Alka says she should talk to someone?
qa.a: She may feel exposed at first, but also cared for, since Alka stayed with her and came along.

grounding: A teacher records how a teenager noticed a friend's constant put-downs, offered specific praise, stayed close and brought her to a trusted adult.

passage:
Friday night.
Lalit did it again at cricket nets. Dropped one catch and said "Useless, I'm always useless" three times, loudly. Then he said no to captaining the Under-16s, even though Coach asked him first. I don't get it. He's the only one who remembers everyone's birthdays. So I told him, not in a gushing way, "You read spin better than anyone. You got Sahil out twice last week." He shrugged, but he stopped muttering. I'm walking with him to nets every day next week. If he's still this down after the holidays, I'll ask if he wants to talk to his chacha, the one he actually listens to. Or I'll tell Coach.
Jahnavi

qa.q: What did Lalit say no to?

qa.q: What does Lalit's "I'm always useless" suggest he feels about himself?

qa.a: Jahnavi gave honest, specific praise about reading spin and getting Sahil out, and planned to walk with Lalit to nets, which gives him real evidence and company.

grounding: A teenager notices a friend's put-downs and refusals, gives specific praise, stays close and plans to involve a trusted adult if the low mood lasts.

passage: Jomon, twenty, stood outside the only tailor's shop in Thodupuzha holding two shirt fabrics and his phone. He had already sent photos to four friends. "Hansa, blue or green?" he called to his cousin, who was buying rice across the road. "Blue," she said. A friend texted "green" a minute later, and Jomon's stomach sank. At the co-op bank where he'd just started as a clerk, the manager had called his ledger "a bit untidy", and he had lain awake all night replaying it. Hansa crossed over. "Which one do you like?" Jomon opened his mouth. Nothing came. "I... don't know." "Then stand here till you do," she said, smiling. "No phones." It took four minutes. Green.

qa.q: How many friends had Jomon sent photos to?
qa.a: He had sent photos to four friends.

qa.q: Why did Jomon's stomach sink when a friend texted "green"?
qa.a: The different opinion made him unsure and anxious, because he relies on others' approval to decide.

qa.q: What small step did Hansa suggest, and why is it useful?
qa.a: She asked what he liked and told him to decide without phones, a small chance to trust his own judgement.

qa.q: How might Hansa see Jomon's habit of asking everyone?
qa.a: She seems fond of him but aware he has lost touch with his own preference, so she nudges him kindly.

grounding: A young man in a small town seeks opinions before a simple choice and is crushed by mild criticism, and his cousin nudges him to find his own view.

passage: In a shared flat in Malmö, Tomas, twenty-one, rewrote his university essay introduction for the fifth time. He'd already asked his flatmate Ulla, his mum and two classmates if it was okay. Ulla said it was fine but "a bit long". For the rest of the evening Tomas barely spoke, feeling like a failure. When his mum replied "Brilliant!", he felt great for about ten minutes, then began doubting again. Around midnight Ulla found him still at the kitchen table. "What do you think of it?" she asked. "I don't know. That's the problem." "Try this. Read it out loud and tell me one thing you're proud of in it. Just you." He read. "The last line. I like the last line." "Good. Start there."

qa.q: How many times had Tomas rewritten his introduction?
qa.a: He rewrote his essay introduction for the fifth time.

qa.q: How did Tomas feel after Ulla said the essay was "a bit long"?
qa.a: He felt crushed and like a failure, barely speaking for the rest of the evening.

qa.q: What turning point did Ulla offer, and why is it useful?
qa.a: She asked him to name one thing he was proud of on his own, which starts building his own sense of worth instead of borrowing it.

qa.q: How might Ulla feel seeing her mild comment upset Tomas so much?
qa.a: She may feel surprised and a little guilty, but she stays kind and helps him look inward.

grounding: A student whose mood rises and falls with others' approval begins, with a flatmate's help, to find his own judgement of his work.
